#181. CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts

Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership

A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.

“Writing to a CEO in this tone and to this intent is an extraordinary step for this union to have to take,” Clancy wrote.

He warned: “Whilst there are legitimate cost pressures facing UKRI, ultimately any cuts will reduce the UK’s national science capability at a time when it is most needed.”

This year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), the government’s infrastructure funding agency, which is part of UKRI, revealed it needed to make £162m in savings by 2030.

While the core budget of the STFC remains broadly flat at about £835m a year, it is under financial pressure as a result of several factors. These include soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates. The last has resulted in an increase in costs relating to international facilities such as Cern.

As a result, in July UKRI released a plan to balance the STFC’s budget by 2030, revealing research projects and national facilities are to face significant changes.

“As responsible custodians of public funds, which I very much view our job is to be, we have to make sure that our costs are in line with our budget and that we don’t overspend the budget available to us,” Chapman said at the time, adding that it was important to prioritise spending in areas that made the biggest scientific impact.

The future of the UK’s largest telescope at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire has been put at risk, while the Diamond Light Source, the Central Laser Facility and the Isis Neutron and Muon Source, all in Oxfordshire, will remain operational but have been told to make efficiency savings.

The Clara facility in Cheshire – one of the world’s most advanced medium-energy electron beam facilities, which develops and tests next-generation accelerator technologies – is to be mothballed.

Clancy wrote in his letter to Chapman: “Our members working at UKRI do vital work which puts our country at the cutting edge of scientific developments and industrial applications and has considerable benefits across high-growth sectors, as well as in medical research and treatment. To pause or ‘mothball’ funding for many of the facilities where they work is to risk permanently losing the expertise that underpins the sector.”

The opening of a voluntary exit scheme to UKRI employees was also flagged by Clancy, who said the scheme was launched in parallel with the STFC cuts and without the requisite consultation on the organisational change plan with the recognised trade unions. His letter urges a pause to enable proper consultation and evidence-gathering on the cuts’ potential impact.

“In the absence of our requests leading to any productive engagement, we have lost confidence in your position as CEO,” Clancy wrote to Chapman.

Prof Leszek Borysiewicz, the chair of UKRI, said the board had full confidence in Chapman and his leadership team.

“We support the direction of the ambitious reform programme UKRI is undertaking to become more effective, agile and better able to respond to the country’s priorities and needs,” Borysiewicz said. “Delivering transformation on this scale is a substantial undertaking involving difficult decisions about how UKRI operates, where resources are focused and how we deliver the greatest impact.

“UKRI has been clear with staff and unions about the direction of change, including its new mission and funding model, greater join-up across programmes and the unification of professional services. The decisions announced this year followed extensive engagement with staff, research and user communities, alongside detailed consideration of the impacts of different funding choices.” The science minister, Chris McDonald, said: “I have full confidence in Ian Chapman’s leadership of UKRI. The organisation’s ongoing and essential transformation programme will ensure projects supported through our record £86bn commitment to R&D will deliver maximum impact and value for money – as the British public rightly expect.

“I know from personal experience that this transformation will have a significant and personal impact on workers and others affected, and we will continue to engage the UKRI workforce. I am committed to working closely with UKRI, the workers, and their trade unions as we continue to progress the transformation plan.”

#178. Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

If antibiotics stop working, even the smallest infection can be fatal. The WHO expects millions of deaths over the next 25 years. Can the "One Health" approach help combat antibiotic resistance?

"The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently. "An estimated cumulative number of 39 million deaths directly attributable to AMR [antimicrobial resistance] would occur in the next 25 years."

It was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added. "When we see the trend, the investments, the action, we don't think we are on the right track."

A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, said Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen. "If antibiotics were no longer effective, modern medicine as we know it today would no longer be possible at all."

Imirzalioglu is not only an expert on antibiotic resistance but also on "One Health," a concept adopted in 2004 by experts in human medicine, veterinary medicine and nature conservation. It recognizes that the health of humans, animals and the environment is closely interconnected.

After all, antibiotics and antimicrobial-resistant germs are not just a problem in hospitals. They can also be found in animal shelters, in animal products, in waste water, in fertilizers and in plants. "One Health tries to keep an eye on all of this," Imirzalioglu said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For hospitals and doctors' offices this means that antibiotics must be used as selectively and purposefully as possible. To this end, research is focused primarily on developing better and faster diagnostic methods.

In Germany, antibiotics were frequently prescribed against respiratory or urinary tract infections, Imirzalioglu said. But antibiotics are only effective against bacteria. If a virus causes the infection, they are ineffective.

Nonetheless, every antibiotics dose has consequences: it damages our gut microbiome. This consists of billions of micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, which are essential for digestion, metabolism and the immune system. "If we damage the [bacteria], resistant pathogens can spread and take their place," Imirzalioglu said.

Another problem was that such a spreading of resistant pathogens in the gut often went unnoticed and without causing symptoms, he added.

So people became "carriers of resistant pathogens, which they, in turn, release back into their environment."

In this way, resistant pathogens make their way out of hospitals via toilets and sinks into wastewater and, from there, into the Baltic Sea, where they are ingested by wild birds. This pathway was traced in a study by Katharina Schaufler, a veterinarian and microbiologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health (HIOH).

Antibiotics have not only been used in humans on a large scale over a long time, excessive use in veterinary medicine has also led to resistance to nearly all available antibiotics, Schaufler said.

In 2006, an EU-wide ban on the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feedcame into effect. Since then, antibiotics may only be applied as part of veterinary treatment.

The problem is that due to factory farming the use of antibiotics for medical purposes is a permanent necessity. The mere fact that animals live together in confined spaces causes infections to spread rapidly.

Lack of space as well as boredom lead the animals to injure each other and this happens in an environment where, in Schaufler's words, "there's already a high level of bacterial pressure."

Through fertilizers, antibiotic-resistant pathogens enter the environment. "It has been proven that, for example, resistant bacteria can still be found on lettuce heads," the veterinarian said. Resistant bacteria were also found time and again on meat.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

National solutions are also falling short. In many countries, antibiotics are still a standard additive in animal feed, Schaufler said. And in such countries, antibiotics could be obtained in drugstores without prescriptions, Imirzalioglu added. Both say that all of this makes the global fight against antibiotic resistance more difficult.

Political will is of the essence when it comes to combating antibiotic resistance. Imirzalioglu works at Guardian, a project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space.

The aim of the project is to prevent outbreaks of diseases caused by resistant bacteria by monitoring and analyzing wastewater in the German state of Hesse.

At EU level, Imirzalioglu is also an advisor at the Antimicrobial Resistance One Health Network. He sums up his experience with policymakers: "The experts and working groups have great ideas, and then these are often scaled back or stifled during the initial stages."

Perhaps the lack of political will so far is one of the reasons why the WHO's Nyemazi is issuing an appeal to every individual: Preventing antibiotic resistance means preventing infections, through hygiene, regular vaccinations and doctor's appointments as well as taking medications in accordance with prescriptions.

#177. ‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post

Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him

Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.”

The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

But the photo with Putin, showing Trump leaning towards the Russian leader to talk to him as they met at the summit, posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform overnight, prompted condemnation in the UK.

Asked for his reaction, Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, the British party most closely associated with Trump, replied: “Horror.”

He told Sky News: “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Asked whether Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, who is a friend of Trump, would speak to the US president about this, Tice replied: “Oh, there have been a number of occasions where one could agree with Trump, and then disagree with him.

“There have been more occasions recently when clearly we have disagreed with him and said so very explicitly. And in a sense, that’s the nature of long friendships. Sometimes you’ll agree and sometimes you’ll disagree. And, I think the disagreements are growing.”

Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices.

Polling last month for YouGov found that just 10% of British people have a favourable opinion of Trump, with 86% holding an unfavourable view. Asked about the “My friend” post, Alex Burghart, Badenoch’s deputy, said he was “very sad” about it.

He told Sky News: “I’m sad and I’m depressed, because the world that I grew up in was one in which the United States was a defender of freedom. I worry that we might be moving into a world where that isn’t the case any more.”

Asked about his party’s previous support for Trump, Burghart replied: “If you look at what the Conservative party is proposing in terms of defence and foreign policy, it’s very clear that we are still on the side of freedom, and we’re the party that has said that we will put up defence spending to what Nato wants it to be.

“So I think you can trust Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives on this. But, I very much hope that we don’t enter a world in which large, aggressive powers feel that they can occupy their neighbours and get the approval of the United States.”

When asked about the Trump post, Hamish Falconer, a Foreign Office minister, called Putin “a butcher” and said Andy Burnham would make the UK’s views known.

Falconer told Sky News: “The prime minister speaks to the president regularly and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”

#175. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, new report shows. Here are the key takeaways

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company launched and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.)

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.)

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

“PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them

Sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge

“I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

A boat capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, the country's emergency agency said on Saturday.

"So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing," said Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency.

The boat was carrying mourners for a burial ceremony from the town of Ayama to Ukubie in the southern Bayelsa State on Friday when it sank.

In August, at least 51 died after a boat capsized in northwest Nigeria's Sokoto State.

In September 2025, a boat carrying over 100 passengers sank in north-central Niger State, leaving dozens dead.

Good morning and welcome to our UK politics blog.

Andy Burnham says these are the first steps towards rebuilding “the bridges broken all of those years ago” with “our nearest neighbours and our largest market”.

While he’s voiced support for re-joining the bloc, he’s also stressed that all options are on the table and there’s a long road ahead in convincing the British public and securing the unanimous assent needed from the 27-nation bloc.

Critics have piled in this morning, warning how tricky of an endeavour this could be. Ex-PM Theresa May, whose government was brought down by Brexit in 2019, has told the BBC that the divorce “is done” and he should “move on”.

That interview’s coming up on Laura Kuenssberg’s show later this morning. Meanwhile over on Sky, Brexiteer Michael Gove is hosting Reform and Tory naysayers as well as the European relations minister. I’ll recap their comments.

I’ll draw the blog to a close for now, here’s a summary of the heated discussion about the new EU deals:

Conservatives and Reform have criticised the deals lifting red tape on food and agricultural products, aligning emissions trading schemes and the youth visas for 100,000 young people from both sides

They say the trade deal will bind British farmers to EU regulations and their “rulebook”

But Foreign Sec Ed Miliband says farmers selling products into the EU – the largest trading market – already face those rules; this just cuts out the “filling out of forms” and red tape involved

He says if the UK is part of the EU again too, it would also get to have a say in shaping the bloc’s standards

Critics say the deal will also bring in young Europeans at a time when one million Brits aged 16-24 aren’t in work or education; they argue they will be taking jobs from British people

Miliband says the deal “goes both ways” – young Brits will also be afforded the opportunity to work and live in Europe after a post- Brexit decade where that generation has received “a pretty raw deal”. He says the government can address the Neets crisis while also giving young people this freedom and opportunity

Ex-PM Theresa May, who resigned after three years of struggling with the Brexit negotiation, says she’s “aghast” that Burnham is touching the topic again. She says the British people voted and Burnham should move on

Burnham’s government says they’re not going to just put up with the Brexit deal that was achieved, which they say left Britain poorer and more isolated.

“If people think the status quo is really good on Brexit and that it’s been great for Britain, well, they won’t like this deal. I think most people think the status quo has been actually pretty rubbish. And we need to make it better, and that’s what this deal does,” said Miliband.

On Sky this morning, the Conservatives and Reform deputy leaders were also asked on if they’d ever enter into an election deal with Restore Britain.

“Given the line that they take on ethno-nationalism, I think that’s very, very unlikely,” said Tory deputy leader Alex Burghart.

Reform was accused by Michael Gove of leaving the door open for a deal with the even – further right Restore. Deputy leader Richard Tice said Reform wasn’t “doing a deal with anybody”.

Labour MP Emily Thornberry then interjected saying: “Labour will never do a deal with Restore. There we are. That’s all you have to say. Reform will never do a deal with Restore. He can’t say it.”

Tice said: “I’m not doing a deal with Rupert Lowe.”

double quotation markOne area where the UK is absolutely and completely united across the whole political spectrum is standing with Ukraine against Russia’s barbaric, illegal war.

double quotation markIt’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator and no-one is in any doubt about that.

Critics of the youth mobility deal have mainly focused on the idea of an “influx” of European youth competing with Brits for jobs when there’s this ongoing Neets crisis.

Miliband on the BBC, points out that the UK already has such youth mobility deals with several countries, and the offer goes both ways.

double quotation markThere’ll be young people from Britain going to work in Europe, and study, and live, and there’ll be young people from Europe coming to our country as well.

I absolutely believe we can both address the issue of Neets, which I think Alan Milburn did excellently this week, and we can address the issue of young people having the freedom to go and work and live in Europe.

I think young people have got a really raw deal over the last decade, and it starts to put it right.

The Tories and Reform have made the argument this morning that the new food deal is “bad” for British farmers, because they will be subject to EU rules and standards.

They say more than 90% of British farmers currently don’t export to the EU- so why should Britain have to cede that control over standards?

The government’s response to this is that well, at the moment, farmers who sell into the EU already have to comply by the rules and also fill out loads of forms to prove they’re matching the standards.

“This is why it’s the worst of both worlds. We have to abide by the rules and fill in all the forms. What is the point of that?” says Ed Miliband on the BBC.

double quotation markWhat we’re saying is that actually, yes, we should integrate into the market where for the first time, we’ll be able to shape decisions agreed to in the EU.

Reform UK’s deputy leader Richard Tice has also slammed the new EU agreements as “a really bad deal”.

Tice doesn’t elaborate on details here, or where that cost will come from but it appears his argument is: “The extra burdens of EU regulations that will be forced through dynamic alignment across all UK businesses is way more than that small net benefit.”

“Yes, a few exporting food businesses may benefit. But what about all the bakers in Boston and Skegness and elsewhere in the country who don’t export to the EU who will then have to suffer dynamic alignment amongst hundreds of thousands of other UK businesses that don’t export.”

A chief concern for the Europeans as to the idea of the UK rejoining the bloc is frankly, the lack of British political stability this past decade, and the fear that a change in government down the line would lead to another backflip.

Burghart this morning went as far as saying that a future Tory government would reverse the deals secured on Friday.

double quotation markWe will certainly repeal this deal. This is a very bad deal.

double quotation markAnd this deal will make a positive impact on both exports and imports, and crucially- this is the point that I noticed the retailers were making - it will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly, pointlessly, as a result of the bad deals that we had.

double quotation markIf people think the status quo is really good on Brexit and that that’s been great for Britain, well, they won’t like this deal. I think most people think the status quo has been actually pretty rubbish. And we need to make it better and that is what this deal does.”

Tory deputy head Alex Burghart has been arguing against the deals on Sky and the BBC this morning. He argues the removal of red tape on food and agricultural products is “really bad for business” as British farmers now will have to follow EU regulations when some don’t even trade with the bloc.

He says this is a “a huge deadweight cost for them”, and that that the EU has added even more regulations in recent years.

He also says that linking the emissions schemes means that “forces the UK to adopt the higher price of carbon that EU puts on businesses”, and he argues that the 100,000 places youth mobility scheme will take jobs away from young Brits.

Gove puts to him that “business is pretty clear, that it’s a good deal” and “almost every supermarket CEO says it will be good for consumers.”

“So you’re setting yourselves against businesses, and cheaper prices.”

Theresa May spent three years as prime minister (2016-2019) trying to negotiate the Brexit deal, before resigning.

She has told the BBC this morning she is “aghast” at the idea of Burnham resurrecting the issue, warning him of the enormous effort ahead:

double quotation markWhat I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it’s across the whole of government. double quotation markAnd that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU.

And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit. When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote.

So I’m afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.

A summit in Brussels this week produced agreements which will:

Allow 100,000 young adults from each side to live and work in the other’s countries for up to three years

Scrap border checks on plant and animal products, which Burnham says will lower the cost of food

Link emissions trading schemes, lowering carbon taxes on some exports

The PM says these first package of deals will create opportunities for young people and keep supermarket prices down. Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Co-op, has been among the supermarket giants welcoming the move for customers.

At Brussels, there were also commitments to keep negotiating other areas. One key subject to be sorted out in the next six months is university fees for European students in the UK and vice versa.

An EU official briefing media said negotiations hadn’t been easy but there had been good will to find solutions.

#169. Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness. Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology. The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw. Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.

Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.

One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.

Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.

Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.

Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.

The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.

NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

A police spokesperson said the force was addressing “areas of learning” and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: “Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.”

The IOPC said the family had a right to ask for a review of the internal investigation and that it had not yet received a request.

#167. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”

This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

#162. ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first foreign bilateral trip since taking office. He is expected to discuss flood recovery, trade and energy in his talks with Modi. DW has more.

Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:

India declared at 720-9, the highest Test total by any team in New Zealand, on day four of the first Test in Wellington.

The innings gave India a 352-run first-innings lead. India's previous best in New Zealand was 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009.

Rishabh Pant struck 128 from 153 balls, his ninth Test century and fourth since returning to Test cricket in 2024. Dhruv Jurel added 78, and the declaration came midway through the second session.

Pant's sixes took him to 108 in Tests, behind only England's Ben Stokes: "I just keep it simple most of the time. Whenever I see the ball, I try to hit it," he said.

New Zealand closed on 119-2, still 233 behind, with Devon Conway unbeaten on 59 and Rachin Ravindra on 27. Jasprit Bumrah dismissed captain Tom Latham for a duck early in the innings, and Henry Nicholls, who made 175 not out in the first innings, fell for 31 to a sharp catch by Jurel off Prasidh Krishna.

New Zealand now need to bat out most of the final day, and India have at least 90 overs to take eight wickets.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to arrive in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March.

The 36-year-old former rapper will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. He will also meet Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and briefly visit President Droupadi Murmu.

Reconstruction after August's devastating floods is expected to dominate the talks. The disaster left some 1,500 dead and more than 5,200 missing, with roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes destroyed.

Nepal estimates rebuilding will cost $4.78 billion.

Nepal is also pressing for an extra route for commercial flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

"India is a major and important partner for Nepal," Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, saying the leaders would discuss trade, transit, investment, energy, connectivity and infrastructure.

New Delhi said the visit "reflects the importance India attaches to its relations with Nepal," AFP reported. Local media reported that talks may also touch upon unresolved border disputes.

India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of its imports, worth $8.6 billion, versus China's 13%, according to World Bank figures. India and China regularly compete for influence in Nepal.

Shah will be accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.

#158. US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court

Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”

Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”

The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.

Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.

In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.

“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.

The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”

Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta said ​he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.

Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

#153. When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories

Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.

Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.

Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.

It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.

In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.

Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.

When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.

She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.

Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.

To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.

Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.

His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

#150. Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.

The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.

India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety ⁠or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.

A video ‌from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.

In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.

An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it ​had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.

“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Reporters Without Borders has ​said the removal of journalistic content from social media ​has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media ​companies hardly any time to review ‌and decide on takedown requests.

In ​February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies ​to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.

Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.

“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.
